Medicine pathway: branch entry criteria, preferred options and “use when” conditions were assigned from this topic's own indications and management steps. Confirm each against the cited guideline before clinical use.

pathophysiology.summary: Malignant bowel obstruction is mechanical or functional blockage of the small or large bowel by intra-abdominal or pelvic cancer (commonly ovarian or colorectal). It may be partial or complete, at one or several levels, and often relapses.
keyMechanisms: Tumour, peritoneal disease or adhesions block the lumen; motility failure from infiltration of mesentery or nerves causes functional obstruction.
Proximal distension → secretion of fluid and electrolytes → more distension, colic and vomiting.
Inflammation and oedema around tumour worsen obstruction — the rationale for dexamethasone (MOH).
Antisecretory drugs (hyoscine butylbromide, octreotide) reduce gut secretions and colic (NICE NG31).

symptoms: Nausea, vomiting (faeculent in low obstruction), colicky and continuous abdominal pain.
Abdominal distension; absent flatus and stool in complete obstruction (some flatus in partial obstruction).
physicalSigns: Distension, tympanic abdomen, visible peristalsis; tinkling or absent bowel sounds.
redFlags: Peritonism, fever, tachycardia — perforation or ischaemia
precipitants: Ovarian, colorectal, gastric or pancreatic cancer with peritoneal disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Loaded rectum or colon on examination or imaging; settles with laxatives.
Recent opioid increase; no transition point.
Previous surgery, no new tumour — may be surgically treatable.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm and decide goals
actions: Confirm obstruction (CT if it will change management) and agree goals with patient and family.
Ask the surgical and oncology teams whether any intervention fits the person's goals — selection criteria were not reviewed in these sources.

clinicalManagement.title: Medical management
actions: Stop prokinetics if there is colic or complete obstruction (metoclopramide label: contraindicated in mechanical obstruction; MOH p. 10).
Antisecretory: hyoscine butylbromide first line; octreotide if no improvement within 24 h (NICE NG31 1.5.22).
Dexamethasone 6–16 mg daily for obstructive syndromes (MOH Protocol-010 p. 4); review within 7 days.
Antiemetic: haloperidol for nausea (MOH); metoclopramide only in partial/functional obstruction without colic (MOH p. 10).
Pain: parenteral (SC/IV) opioid — oral opioid labels list GI obstruction as a contraindication; use SC route with specialist advice.
Hydration: discuss clinically assisted hydration and review benefit or harm at least every 12 h (NICE NG31 1.4).

patientEducation: Explain that obstruction may settle and recur.
Small sips and mouth care; venting options if vomiting persists.
lifestyleAndDiet: Sips of fluid and small soft meals as tolerated when partially obstructed.
mdtReferrals: Surgical and oncology review for intervention options.
dischargeCriteria: Symptoms controlled for the chosen place of care, or safe transfer arranged.
Patient and family know the plan, the medicines and whom to call.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at least daily; reassess goals if obstruction resolves or recurs.
